tweets.text:
About a week ago I was hiking with my family when my mum went to the bathroom and let out a visceral, horror movie scream. Something I've never heard in my entire life.

I didn't have time to think. Purely out of reflex, my body sprinted towards her. My dad reacted the same way. There was no thought, no bravery, no decision. We were completely unable to do anything other than run to her.

There was no real danger. A frog had simply jumped on her while she was on the toilet.

But I've been pondering it ever since, because I think it answered a prayer.

A few weeks earlier, I had been thinking about how much pain Jesus took. Betrayal, torture, humiliation, then a prolonged agony ending in death. Hours of some of the most brutal pain in history, in front of his own mother and loved ones.

And Jesus said that at any time he could have called on legions of angels to save him. He didn't. I couldn't understand that. How can anyone go through such agony, with a way out, and not take it? Does he really love us that much?

So I started praying to understand his pain. I was too scared to ask for that outright, so I hedged. I asked for 0.1% of it, or whatever he knows I can handle. Then I spent my travels on edge, waiting. Would I get stung by a rockfish while diving, bitten by a snake, tear a ligament on a hike?

I was looking for the wrong answer. I think God looked at my heart posture when I prayed. I didn't need to feel physical pain, because what I sought was to understand his nature a little better. To understand how his love transcends pain to the point of enabling the miracle of the cross.

When my mother screamed as if a tiger was attacking her, I couldn't have, in any timeline, reacted any other way than to rush to her. I can't logically explain it other than as a reflex of love, which perhaps is God's nature showing through me, and through my father, in that instant.

It sounds a bit dramatic given the frog. But that was a one-second glimpse, with no time to think. Jesus had hours, with every chance to reconsider.

He is eternal, and his nature doesn't change. If Jesus and the Father are one, then that explains the cross. He is love, and love transcends all other options. So even with the way out in front of him, he loved us, and he would never forsake us.

Bitcoin is on track for something it has never done: two red years in a row.

2025: -6.3%, closing at $87,496
2026 so far: -31.3%, at about $60,100

Every previous losing year was followed by a gain:

2014: -56%, then 2015: +34%
2018: -73%, then 2019: +94%

Bitcoin's yearly pattern is being tested for the first time.
